“your product looks too polished to be vibecoded.” i’ve heard that a lot about caltodo . the funny part? it basically was. here’s exactly how i designed the UX/UI: 1. copy websites you love and combine them 2. use 21st .dev for animations and buttons that’s it. in the age of vibecoding, something interesting is happening: if your product looks vibecoded, people trust it less. so the bar is no longer just building fast. the bar is taste. for caltodo, i pulled inspiration from Notion , Apple , TickTick , and ckpnt . then remixed those patterns into something i personally wanted to use. almost every great interface works like this. taste → remix → iteration. don’t be afraid to copy. just make sure the final product feels like you. now available for all schools at caltodo.me 👨‍💻

From my late 20s to my late 30s, I was a struggling entrepreneur that went to bed praying for 1 thing: Opportunity. Somebody willing to look at a 28 year old with no network, no credibility and no experience, and give him a fair shot. Out of college I spent 3 years modernizing my father's factory. I was fortunate to have been running around the factory floor since I was a teenager. It was where I learned about shipping, receiving, accounting, and where I realized what my biggest passion was: data. I wanted to understand how to use data to improve a business. At the time, nothing was on the web yet, but I knew it would change everything. So I taught myself to build servers, and eventually started a company from a closet in LA. My vision was to build a centralized software system for computer manufacturing companies, where: 1. For each computer sold, customers would be forced to auto-register it with their name and information upon unboxing 2. This way, the the manufacturer gets customer data, routed into a database, then connected to their call center and return facilities. 3. When the customer calls because something broke, the company easily identifies them, their device, and what failed. As many entrepreneurs know, you can have a great idea and a great solution. But without the opportunity, it never comes to fruition. Here's how it unfolded: 1999. I wrote 50 letters to every venture capitalist in Silicon Valley. Got 7 or 8 meetings. Flew up, pitched, got rejected by all of them. This created a capital constraint for my business that ended up teaching me the raw skills I needed (leveraged buyouts, high yield debt). 1999. I finally found 3 customers willing to try my software. All 3 said the same thing: we'll buy it, but only if you take over the customer service operation behind it. I said yes, mostly because I knew that sitting that close to the people using the product would make it better. Then I realized I had only $10,000 to start. So I went back and said, "I'm just starting and I don't have the capital." All 3 paid me between 3 and 9 months in advance. 2000. A global brand handed my team of 5 its warehousing and support operations across Asia, the US and Europe. We had 60 days to stand it up. On weekends I was driving a scissor lift around a 60,000 square foot warehouse, running cable from the server room to the receiving dock while the engineers wrote the application. I ran that business for the next 27 years, grew it to $2B and 100,000+ employees, and never took a dollar of outside capital. In 30-some years, I don't think an opportunity has ever presented itself to me at the opportune time. So the order I settled on was this: Pray for opportunity. Respect the opportunity. Deliver against it. Last month I became CEO of Crescendo. I get to spend this opportunity on the problem I know best, with a team that's built this category before. So excited for this new chapter 🚀

One of my direct reports had 13K unread recruiting emails. That’s why I outbound to candidates the same way I outbound to enterprise accounts. My response rate is 63%. Here’s what that looks like: 1/ find their actual work For an engineer, I read their PRs and blog posts before I write. For a marketer, I read their landing pages. For an AE, I dig into who they actually talk with. Then I reference something specific in the outreach. Something like: “I saw you were the only marketer during the Series B announcement. That type of ownership is who we’re looking for.” That kind of specificity cannot be spray-and-pray. 2/ reach out on more than one channel I’ll message candidates on 2-3 channels within a week (LinkedIn, email, whatever platform they’re active on). Same message shape, but matching the medium. These are busy people, and often messages will get missed. 3/ stay in touch even when the answer is no If someone takes a call and it’s not the right fit right now, I stay in contact. Send them things I think they’d like. Introduce them to people. These are the kind of people I want to know. What breaks through is the same thing that breaks through in an enterprise deal: Someone did their homework, reach out through the right channels, and treated the relationship like it was worth building whether or not it converted right now.

We are giving 5 undergraduate students $15,000 each to build an impact project next summer. This summer, I was privileged enough to receive a grant from Nazan.Love to research AI displacement in the workforce, and I decided to focus on how I could help prepare my generation to enter it. What I found is that the codified, rules-based tasks that fill the first year of an entry-level job are the ones considered most at risk, and they happen to be exactly what the college conveyor belt puts students on. Then I started talking to my classmates about their conveyor belt internships, and learned that this isn't the work many of them want to do. This wasn’t very surprising, as my freshman year at Brown was full of people arguing about how best to fix systems, and about their own solutions to real problems. Now most have drifted into built-in pipelines, which are unfortunately the only paths on campus with real infrastructure. This made me think: can we help young people build what they came to college wanting to do? With the gracious support of Shervin Talieh , Diego Castillo and I are building Tyche Fellows to do just that. The grant replaces summer internship income, so undergraduates can spend the summer building rather than recruiting. We want to back the person more than the pitch, with a preference for students who have lived closest to the problem they want to solve. We are still shaping what the summer will look like. If you’re a student with something you want to build, or an operator/funder who aligns with our vision, feel free to reach out :) Application opens in September. tychefellows.com
